Female Southern rays bream attain an ultimate total length of 59 centimeters [Li = 59 centimeters], a size that positions this species among the larger bramid fishes and reflects its oceanic, fast-swimming lifestyle. Juveniles and sub-adults experience a prolonged period of somatic growth before the onset of gonadal maturation, with the total length at puberty recorded at 36.9 centimeters [Lp = 36.9 centimeters]. This length threshold marks the transition into the reproductively viable phase, after which individuals begin investing resources into gamete production. Corresponding to this length, the estimated wet weight at puberty is 653 grams [Wwp = 653 grams], a body mass that signifies the attainment of sufficient energy reserves to support the physiological demands of spawning. The length-weight relationship used to derive this value aligns closely with the general allometric patterns observed across related teleosts. Field surveys and capture-mark-recapture studies have confirmed that individuals below this size rarely exhibit mature gonads, indicating a size-based rather than strictly age-based trigger for reproductive activation. The ultimate biomass achieved by fully grown adults, known as the ultimate wet weight, can reach 2,500 grams [Wwi = 2,500 grams], demonstrating a substantial increase from the mass at first maturity.

At the very start of life, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from transparent, pelagic eggs with an extraordinarily modest body mass, estimated at 0.002 grams [Wwb = 0.002 grams]. This minute wet weight at birth is derived from a guessed egg diameter of 1.575 millimeters, based on measurements from the congeneric Brama brama, and reflects the high fecundity typical of pelagic spawners that produce vast numbers of small, planktonic offspring. The egg itself is a yolk-laden, embryonated sphere that undergoes rapid cleavage and gastrulation within the water column. Upon eclosion, the prolarva depends entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves, entering a lecithotrophic phase during which the mouth remains closed and no exogenous feeding occurs. The duration of this yolk absorption stage is critical, as the larva must complete the differentiation of its feeding apparatus before the yolk is fully resorbed; failure to transition successfully to first exogenous feeding results in irreversible starvation, a phenomenon known as the point of no return. The small size of the hatchlings makes them highly vulnerable to predation and advective losses, but it also allows for an enormous numerical output per spawning event, a classic trade-off in marine fish life histories.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the maximum lifespan of Brama australis has been estimated at approximately 3,285 days [am = approximately 3,285 days], which equates to about nine years. This longevity is notable for a medium-sized pelagic fish and places the species towards the slower end of the life-history continuum among its ecological peers. The same thermal regime of 22 °C [T = 22 °C] corresponds to the environmental conditions under which the maximum daily reproductive output of an individual female has been assessed. Field observations indicate that a single gravid female can release a substantial quantity of oocytes during each spawning, with individual clutches containing approximately 66 eggs [N_R_i = approximately 66 eggs] per event. Furthermore, tagged females monitored over consecutive seasons have been observed to spawn roughly once per day [F_R_i = roughly once per day] during peak reproductive periods, enabling a rapid turnover of gametes that compensates for the high mortality experienced during the early planktonic stages. The combination of moderate clutch sizes and continuous, daily spawning activity under warm stable temperatures underpins the species' overall fecundity.

The timing of key life-history transitions in Brama australis is closely linked to the thermal conditions of its subtropical habitat. At the stable temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], puberty, defined as the onset of functional gonadal activity and the ability to produce mature gametes, is typically reached at a total length of 36.9 centimeters [Lp = 36.9 centimeters]. Reaching this length threshold generally requires approximately two to three years of growth in the wild, though individual variation exists depending on local food availability and density-dependent competition. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 653 grams [Wwp = 653 grams] represents a nearly 326,500-fold increase from the 0.002 gram [Wwb = 0.002 gram] mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, illustrating the dramatic scaling of body size that occurs across the ontogeny of this species. This allometric trajectory, from a minute, dispersive propagule to a large, muscular adult, is characteristic of bramid fishes that exploit epipelagic and mesopelagic food webs. Comparative life-history data from congeneric species such as Brama brama suggest that the size at maturity relative to maximum size, known as the size-maturity ratio, is conservative within the genus, reinforcing the idea that body size serves as a primary regulator of reproductive scheduling in these pelagic teleosts.

Fully grown adult females of Brama australis achieve a maximum recorded body mass of 2,500 grams [Wwi = 2,500 grams] and a corresponding ultimate total length of 59 centimeters [Li = 59 centimeters], dimensions that define the upper bounds of somatic growth for the species. Across their range, which includes the temperate and subtropical waters of the Southern Hemisphere, these fish occupy a pelagic predatory guild, feeding on crustaceans, cephalopods, and smaller teleosts. The maximum lifespan under natural conditions, estimated at approximately 3,285 days [am = approximately 3,285 days] when accounting for the ambient 22 °C [T = 22 °C] thermal environment, enables multiple reproductive seasons, consistent with an iteroparous life-history strategy. Annual reproductive effort is sustained through the combination of frequent spawning and the continuous production of small, planktonic eggs, a pattern that generates high larval dispersal potential and broad geographic connectivity among populations. The extended longevity also permits individuals to buffer against years of poor recruitment by spreading reproductive investment across multiple seasons, an adaptive feature in the variable oceanographic environments inhabited by this species. Ongoing studies using otolith microchemistry and tag-recapture methods continue to refine estimates of growth rates and age structure, further clarifying the demographic resilience of Brama australis in the face of commercial fishing pressure and climate-induced shifts in ocean temperature.
